notes.title: Which of the five workflow shapes before you reach for a loop
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§3 Control Flow & Orchestration)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The five patterns, named and drawn — the source this note picks between — Building Effective AI Agents (Anthropic)

  • Routing and handoff as an orchestration primitive in a production SDK — OpenAI Agents SDK — handoffs

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Agents-vs-Workflows — predefined code paths versus model-directed control.

  • Orchestrator-Worker Pattern — the fourth shape in its own right, and its multi-agent form.

  • concurrency and parallelism — how parallel branches actually execute.

What this note adds: the five shapes as a menu you choose from in the round — the single question that selects each one, what it costs, and the one that is secretly an agent. The concept notes own the patterns individually; nothing owns the selection.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The five? Chaining · routing · parallelization · orchestrator-workers · evaluator-optimizer.
What selects chaining? The steps are fixed and ordered, and each one's output feeds the next.
Which one is secretly an agent? Orchestrator-workers — the LLM decides the breakdown at runtime.
Two flavours of parallelization? Sectioning (split the work) and voting (same work N times, aggregate).
When is evaluator-optimizer wasted? When the evaluator can't be grounded — then it's cost for a correlated opinion.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Before I reach for a loop I try to fit the task to one of five fixed shapes. Chaining if the steps are ordered and known. Routing if the first decision is "which kind of request is this". Parallelization if subtasks are independent, or if I want N attempts voted on. Orchestrator-workers if the breakdown itself has to be decided at runtime — and that one is really an agent, so I say so out loud. Evaluator-optimizer if there's a check worth looping against. The value of naming the shape is that four of the five have bounded step counts, which means bounded cost and a testable graph.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Prompt chaining Steps are fixed, ordered, and each output feeds the next. Latency is the sum of every step; a bad early step poisons the rest. The brief reads as "first…, then…, finally…".
Routing Inputs fall into distinct classes that want different handling. A misroute is silent and lands the request in the wrong specialist path. Categories already exist — intents, queues, ticket types.
Parallelization Subtasks are independent (sectioning), or you want N attempts aggregated (voting). Voting multiplies token cost by N; sectioning needs a merge step that can conflict. "For each of these…", or accuracy matters more than cost.
Orchestrator-workers The breakdown can't be written in advance — it depends on the input. This is agency: variable steps, variable cost, and reliability now compounds. You cannot draw the graph without knowing the specific request.
Evaluator-optimizer There's a check worth looping against and clear criteria for "better". Doubles cost per iteration, and loops forever without a cap and a grounded check. A verifier exists, or a human reviewer's criteria are writable.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Chaining A linear graph; optionally a gate between steps that can fail fast. Cost and p95 are the sum of a known number of calls — fully predictable. Failures name a step. Each step gets its own eval.
Routing A classifier node in front, then disjoint downstream paths. Cheap: one small classification call, then one path's cost — not all paths. Misroute rate becomes a first-class metric, per class.
Parallelization A fan-out and a merge node; the merge is where conflicts surface. Latency is the slowest branch; cost is the sum of all branches. Partial failure handling: does one dead branch fail the run or degrade it?
Orchestrator-workers The full harness — loop, step cap, checkpointer, per-step tracing. Unbounded until you cap it; context re-billed each step, so cost grows ~steps². You're operating an agent now: loop detection, budgets, trace review.
Evaluator-optimizer A cycle between generator and evaluator, plus an iteration cap. Roughly 2× per iteration; the cap sets the worst case. Watch iterations-to-accept. Rising means the criteria drifted.

The redraw test: four of these five are drawable as a fixed graph before you see a single request. The fifth isn't, and that's precisely the line between a workflow and an agent.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Bounded versus unbounded, which is the whole reason to prefer a shape. For a fixed workflow of n steps the run cost is simply the sum of its calls, and p95 is the sum of the step p95s. For an orchestrator-workers loop, neither is knowable in advance — you get a distribution whose tail is set by the step cap.

The reliability difference this buys. Compounding applies to both, but the exponent is fixed in a workflow. At p_step = 0.97:

4-step chain   → 0.97^4  ≈ 0.89
12-step loop   → 0.97^12 ≈ 0.69

Same per-step quality, twenty points of end-to-end task success — bought by knowing the step count rather than by improving the model.

When voting is worth its multiple. Voting runs the same task N times and aggregates. It's worth the N× cost only when errors are independent, because correlated errors just get voted for confidently. The honest test to run: sample fifty failures and check whether the majority of runs fail the same way. If they do, voting buys nothing and the money belongs in a verifier instead.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["📋 The task"] --> B{"🔀 Can I write the<br/>steps down now?"}
    B -->|"no"| C(["🔁 Orchestrator-workers<br/>— this is an agent"])
    B -->|"yes"| D{"🔀 Do inputs fall into<br/>distinct classes?"}
    D -->|"yes"| E(["🔀 Routing"])
    D -->|"no"| F{"🔀 Are subtasks<br/>independent?"}
    F -->|"yes"| G(["⚡ Parallelization"])
    F -->|"no"| H{"🔀 Is there a check<br/>worth looping against?"}
    H -->|"yes"| I(["♻️ Evaluator-optimizer"])
    H -->|"no"| J(["➡️ Prompt chaining"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#FCA5A5,stroke:#F87171,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style I fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style J fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The questions, in order:

  1. Can I write the steps down now? No promotes straight to orchestrator-workers, and I name it as agency rather than letting it arrive quietly.

  2. Do inputs fall into classes? Routing first, because it's the cheapest shape that removes the most complexity — each downstream path then gets a simpler prompt and its own eval.

  3. Are subtasks independent? Sectioning if the work splits; voting if it doesn't but accuracy matters more than cost.

  4. Is there a check worth looping against? Only then evaluator-optimizer. Without a grounded check it's a critic loop, which is cost for a correlated opinion — see Reflexion & Self-Critique.

These compose. A production system is often routing at the front, chaining inside two branches, and an agent in the third — and saying that is a stronger answer than picking one.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Quality is fine but it costs five times what we modelled, and nobody can say why a given request was expensive."

Root cause. The team had built an orchestrator-workers shape because it was the pattern their framework's tutorial used. The actual workload was three clearly distinct request types, each with a fixed procedure — a routing workflow with three short chains behind it. Because the breakdown was delegated to the model, every request paid planning tokens to rediscover a structure that was already known, and the step count varied per request for no reason the traces could explain.

Fix. A small classifier at the front and three fixed chains behind it. Cost per request became predictable because the step count stopped being a model output, and per-class evals became possible for the first time. The work was about a week, and all of it was avoidable by asking "can I write the steps down?" before choosing the pattern.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You named routing. Why not just put everything in one prompt and let the model handle all the cases?

Because a prompt that handles five cases is a prompt that's mediocre at five cases. Splitting on the classification lets each downstream path carry only its own instructions and its own few-shot examples, which measurably raises quality per path and makes each one separately evaluable.

The second reason is operational. When the combined prompt regresses, I learn that "the system got worse". When a routed path regresses, I learn which class broke, and I can gate that path's eval in CI without re-running everything.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Orchestrator-workers is the most flexible. Why not start there and simplify later?

Because flexibility here means the step count is a model output, and everything I care about — cost, p95, end-to-end success — is a function of step count. Starting there means launching without being able to state any of those numbers, and the simplification path is bad: once control flow lives in the model the steps were never written down, so simplifying means reconstructing them from traces.

The direction that works is the opposite. Fixed shape first, measure the fall-through, and promote the cases that genuinely need runtime decomposition. That way the agent inherits a known baseline to beat rather than being the baseline.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The routing classifier is now wrong 8% of the time and the categories keep multiplying. What do you do?

First I separate the two problems, because they have different fixes. Category proliferation usually means the taxonomy is describing outputs rather than handling — if two classes flow through the same path, they aren't different classes for routing purposes, and merging them removes the confusion without touching the model.

For the residual error I'd add a confidence threshold and a default path rather than trying to make the classifier perfect. A low-confidence request goes to the most general handler, which is slower and more expensive but correct, and the misroutes I actually care about are the confident-and-wrong ones. Those I'd catch by sampling routed requests against the downstream outcome — a path that escalates far more than its peers is usually receiving traffic it wasn't built for.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design a system where the shape itself has to change as the product learns.

I'd make the shape a configuration artifact rather than code structure, because the thing that changes is which path a class of request takes and how many steps it's allowed. That means a declarative graph — nodes, edges, caps — versioned alongside the prompts and tools it references, so a shape change is a reviewable diff rather than a deploy of new control flow.

The migration mechanism matters more than the representation. New shapes go out as shadow runs on live traffic first, judged on task success and cost per success rather than on eye-balling outputs, then canary a slice. That's the only honest way to tell whether promoting a chain to an agent actually bought coverage, because the failure mode is a shape that looks more capable and performs the same for four times the money.

What I'd resist is making the shape itself model-selected at runtime. That collapses every shape into orchestrator-workers with extra steps, and gives up the one property the fixed shapes exist to provide.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Orchestrator-workers is a workflow pattern, so it's still a workflow."

✅ Reality: It's the one shape where the LLM decides the decomposition at runtime, which is the definition of agency. It belongs on the list because it's the natural promotion target, but choosing it means accepting variable steps, variable cost and compounding reliability — say that when you pick it.

❌ Trap: "Parallelization makes it faster, so it's a free win."

✅ Reality: It trades cost for latency. Sectioning pays for every branch whether or not you needed them all; voting multiplies cost by N and only helps when errors are independent. Latency improves; the bill does not.

❌ Trap: "Evaluator-optimizer is how you add quality."

✅ Reality: It's how you add iterations. Quality only improves if the evaluator is grounded in something checkable; against a correlated critic you pay double to be confidently wrong more slowly. Check that the evaluator has ground truth before you draw the cycle.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Agents-vs-Workflows — the line this note sits just below.

  • Orchestrator-Worker Pattern — the fifth shape, owned in full.

  • Reflexion & Self-Critique — the mechanism behind evaluator-optimizer.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Which rung of the ladder — this note is that decision's workflow rung, resolved into a specific shape.

  • §1 Is there a verifier — decides whether evaluator-optimizer is available to you at all.

  • §6 Orchestrator-worker topology — choosing shape five is the entry point to the multi-agent section.

  • §8 Hard budgets — four shapes give you a step count for free; the fifth is why the cap exists.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — routing on intent, then fixed chains, is usually the right first answer.

  • §14 Deep research agent — sectioning plus an orchestrator is the canonical shape.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — the whole problem is picking a shape rather than building an agent.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • ReWOO's claim — decoupling reasoning from observation to cut token use — ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations (arXiv 2305.18323)

  • The interleaved reason-act loop these are measured against — ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting (arXiv 2210.03629)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Comparison-of-patterns — the three patterns side by side.

  • ReAct · Plan-and-Execute · ReWOO — Reasoning Without Observation — each in full.

What this note adds: what picks one in a round. The comparison note lays the three out; this gives the single property of the task that selects each, the token arithmetic that makes ReWOO interesting, and the failure each one produces when chosen wrong.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The selecting property? Whether step N+1 depends on step N's result.
ReAct's cost? Context re-billed each step — cost grows ~steps².
ReWOO's trade? Plans all calls up front; cheap and parallel, but blind to results.
Plan-and-Execute's failure? Brittle plans — a wrong early assumption executes to the end.
The hybrid that usually wins? Plan once, execute with a bounded repair loop.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The property that picks one is whether the next step depends on the last result. If it genuinely does — debugging, investigation, search — I use an interleaved ReAct loop and accept that context is re-billed each step. If the steps are knowable up front I plan once and execute, which makes cost and latency predictable and lets independent calls run in parallel. ReWOO is the extreme of that: plan every call before seeing any result, substitute the outputs at the end. It's dramatically cheaper and completely blind, so I use it when the tool calls are independent and I'd never have re-planned anyway.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
ReAct — interleaved reason/act Next action genuinely depends on the last observation. Accumulated context re-billed per step; loop drift; variable step count. "Investigate", "debug", "find out why".
Plan-and-Execute Steps are knowable up front but may need mid-course correction. A brittle plan — a wrong assumption at step 1 executes all the way down. The task decomposes cleanly and the decomposition is stable.
ReWOO — plan all calls, substitute later Calls are independent of each other's results. Total blindness to observations; no recovery within the run. A fixed set of lookups that could all have run at once.
Plan + bounded repair (the usual answer) You want predictability but can't guarantee the plan survives contact. A repair budget and the complexity of two modes. Plans mostly hold, and failures are recoverable.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
ReAct A loop with a step cap, loop detection, and per-step tracing. Unbounded until capped; context accumulation is the dominant term. Step-count distribution is the health signal; drift is the failure.
Plan-and-Execute A planner node, then an executor over a fixed list. One planning call, then bounded execution. Predictable p95. Plan quality becomes separately evaluable from execution.
ReWOO Planner emits all calls with placeholders; a solver substitutes results. Lowest token cost — observations never re-enter the planner. Nothing recovers mid-run; failures surface at the end, whole.
Plan + repair Executor can return to the planner within a repair budget. Planning plus a bounded number of re-plans. Re-plan rate is the metric — rising means the planner is guessing.

The redraw test: ReAct is a cycle; Plan-and-Execute is a planner feeding a list; ReWOO is a planner feeding a solver with no edge back. If all three look the same in your diagram, the choice hasn't been made.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why ReAct costs what it does. Each step re-sends the accumulated trajectory, so input tokens grow roughly linearly with step index and total cost with the square of step count. A twelve-step ReAct run doesn't cost twelve times a one-step run — it costs substantially more, and that superlinearity is the entire motivation for the other two patterns.

ReWOO's claim. The paper reports substantial token reduction against ReAct on the benchmarks it evaluates, by never feeding observations back into the reasoning model — the planner emits the full call graph with placeholders, tools execute, and a solver assembles the answer once. The saving is real and the mechanism is obvious; the limitation is just as obvious, which is that no result can influence any decision.

The honest selection test. Take twenty representative traces and count how often a step's arguments actually depended on a previous step's result, rather than merely following it in time. If that fraction is low, you're paying ReAct's accumulation cost for adaptivity you don't use, and planning up front is strictly better. If it's high, ReWOO cannot work for this task no matter what it saves.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["📋 The task"] --> B{"🔀 Do later calls depend on<br/>earlier results?"}
    B -->|"never"| C(["⚡ ReWOO — plan all, substitute"])
    B -->|"sometimes"| D{"🔀 Can a bad plan be<br/>detected mid-run?"}
    B -->|"always"| E(["🔁 ReAct — interleaved loop"])
    D -->|"yes"| F(["🗺️ Plan + bounded repair"])
    D -->|"no"| G(["📝 Plan-and-Execute, and validate the plan"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The question to ask out loud is the first one, and it's worth asking about arguments rather than about order. Steps that merely happen in sequence don't need a loop; steps whose parameters come from a previous result do.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It spent forty steps and eleven dollars concluding it couldn't find the answer."

Root cause. A research agent ran a ReAct loop with a generous step cap. The question had no answer in the available sources, but ReAct has no notion of "the plan is exhausted" — each step saw an incomplete trajectory and reasonably proposed another search. Because observations accumulated in context, every additional step also cost more than the one before, so the most expensive steps were the least productive ones at the end.

Fix. A planning step up front that enumerated the sources worth checking, execution over that list, and a single repair round if the plan came back empty — after which the agent reported that the sources didn't cover the question. The pattern change mattered less than what it forced: a plan makes "exhausted" representable, and a loop with no plan has no way to know it's done.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

ReAct is the standard agent loop. Why would you not use it?

Because its strength — deciding the next action from the last observation — is only worth its cost when the dependency is real. A lot of tasks have steps that follow one another in time without depending on each other's results, and for those ReAct pays accumulation cost for adaptivity that never gets used.

The other reason is predictability. ReAct's step count is an output of the run, so cost and p95 are distributions rather than numbers. If the brief has a latency budget, a planned shape lets me state a figure instead of a range.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

ReWOO saves a lot of tokens. Why isn't it the default?

Because it trades away all recovery. The planner commits to every call before seeing any result, so a wrong assumption in the plan produces a confidently assembled wrong answer with no point at which anything could have noticed. That's acceptable when the calls are genuinely independent lookups and unacceptable the moment one call's output should have changed another's arguments.

There's a subtler issue: ReWOO's plan quality carries the whole run, so it tends to need a stronger and more expensive planner. Some of the token saving comes back as a bigger model on the one call that matters.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At 100× volume, which of these degrades worst and what do you do?

ReAct, because its cost is superlinear per run and its step count has a long tail. At scale the tail dominates the bill — a small fraction of runs going to the step cap can outweigh everything else — and it's also where the timeouts live.

The move I'd make isn't to abandon it but to stratify: plan up front, execute the planned steps, and fall back to a bounded ReAct loop only for the cases the plan didn't resolve. That keeps adaptivity where it earns its cost and removes it from the majority that never needed it. The metric that tells you it's working is the share of runs that touch the fallback path — if it's most of them, the planner is the problem, not the pattern.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design a system where the pattern is chosen per request rather than fixed.

I'd route on the dependency property rather than on task type, because that's what actually selects. A cheap classifier labels the request as independent-lookups, decomposable, or exploratory, and each label maps to ReWOO, plan-and-execute, or ReAct. The classifier is small and its errors are recoverable in one direction — over-promoting to ReAct costs money, under-promoting produces a bad answer — so I'd bias it toward the adaptive shape when uncertain.

The engineering requirement is that all three share a tool layer and a trace schema, so a request that starts planned and falls back to a loop doesn't cross a boundary. That also makes the comparison measurable: same task, same tools, three shapes, judged on cost per successful task.

What I'd watch is the distribution shifting over time. If exploratory grows, either the corpus is degrading or the questions are getting harder, and both are worth knowing before the bill says so.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "ReAct is what an agent is — the others are optimisations."

✅ Reality: ReAct is one control-flow pattern with a specific cost profile. Plan-and-Execute and ReWOO are different answers to the same question about where control lives. Treating ReAct as the definition is how teams end up paying accumulation cost on tasks with no result dependency at all.

❌ Trap: "Planning up front is less capable — the agent can't adapt."

✅ Reality: It can, if you give it a bounded repair loop. Plan-and-execute with re-planning keeps most of the predictability and most of the adaptivity; the pure form is a simplification, not the pattern's ceiling.

❌ Trap: "ReWOO's token saving makes it the obvious choice for cost-sensitive work."

✅ Reality: The saving is real and so is the blindness. It's the right pattern for independent calls and the wrong one anywhere a result should influence a later decision — and cost-sensitive work is often exactly where a wrong answer is most expensive.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Comparison-of-patterns — the three patterns, compared in full.

  • Planning failure modes — brittle plans and drift, which are the failure modes here.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §3 Which workflow shape — this note is that decision continued once you're past the workflow rungs.

  • §8 Hard budgets — ReAct is why a step cap exists; the planned shapes bound themselves.

  • §9 Latency — a plan enables parallel execution, which is the biggest latency lever available.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — plan, parallel execute, bounded repair is the canonical answer.

  • §14 Coding agent — genuinely ReAct: every edit's result changes the next action.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The graph as a state machine, with checkpointing at each super-step — LangGraph: persistence

  • Durable execution, interrupts and resume from a node — LangGraph: durable execution

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • State Machines & Explicit Control Flow for Reliability — why explicit transitions are more reliable than a free loop.

  • LangGraph — Graph as State Machine — nodes, edges and state in a concrete implementation.

What this note adds: what you give up by making it explicit, which the reliability argument doesn't dwell on — and the point at which a graph stops being control flow and becomes a maintenance surface nobody wants to touch.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What a graph buys? Named terminations, testable transitions, and a resume point per node.
What it costs? Every path must be anticipated; novel routes are unreachable.
The honest hybrid? A graph whose nodes contain small bounded loops.
When a free loop is right? The path is genuinely unknown and the step cap is the only bound available.
The signal a graph has gone wrong? Edges added per incident; nobody will delete one.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

An explicit graph gives me named termination conditions, transitions I can unit-test, and a checkpoint boundary per node — which is what makes resume and human approval possible at all. The cost is that the graph can only go where I drew an edge, so genuinely novel paths are unreachable. My default is a graph at the top level with small bounded loops inside individual nodes: the shape is explicit where it matters for reliability, and adaptive where the work actually is. A pure free loop is right only when the path is unknowable, and then the step cap is doing all the work a graph would have done.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Explicit graph Paths are enumerable; you need resume, HITL, or testable transitions. Every path anticipated in advance; edge count grows with edge cases. The flow can be drawn before seeing a request.
Free loop + step cap The path is genuinely unknown and bounded only by budget. No named terminations — the cap is the only stop, and it's arbitrary. "Investigate until you find it."
Graph with loops in nodes (default) Structure at the top, adaptivity inside a step. Two levels to reason about when debugging. Most real systems: a known pipeline with one uncertain stage.
Graph generated per request The structure varies by input but is knowable once the input is read. A generator to maintain, and no static graph to test. Plan-and-execute where the plan is the graph.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Graph Named nodes and edges; a checkpoint per super-step; interrupts at edges. Step count bounded by structure rather than by a cap. Failures name a node. Transitions get unit tests.
Free loop A loop with a cap, loop detection and per-iteration tracing. Unbounded to the cap; the cap sets your worst-case bill. Failures name "the agent". Debugging is trace reading.
Graph + node loops Both, with the loop's bound local to the node. Bounded overall; variability confined to one stage. Two metrics: path distribution, and iterations within the loopy node.
Generated graph A planner emitting a graph, then a generic executor. Planning call plus bounded execution. You test the generator, not the graphs — a harder testing story.

The redraw test: a graph is the diagram — nodes and edges are the picture. A free loop is one box with an arrow back to itself, which is why it's so easy to draw and so hard to operate.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

What the graph actually buys, in reliability terms. A free loop's step count is a distribution with a tail at the cap, so p^N has a variable exponent and the worst case is the cap. A graph's longest path is a property you can read off the structure, which turns end-to-end success from an estimate into a calculation: enumerate the path, multiply the per-node success rates, and you have a number before launch rather than after.

Where the resume value shows up. Checkpointing at node boundaries means a crash costs the current node, not the run. For a twelve-node run that fails at node ten, resume costs one node instead of ten — and the saving is not just tokens but wall-clock, which is what matters when a human is waiting or a nightly job has a window.

The maintenance signal to watch. Count edges added per month against incidents closed. A graph that grows an edge per incident is encoding individual failures rather than structure, and that's the point where it becomes a liability: nobody can say which edges are load-bearing, so nobody deletes any. When that ratio approaches one, the honest move is to collapse those edges into a node containing a bounded loop and let the model handle the variation.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["📋 The flow"] --> B{"🔀 Can I enumerate<br/>the paths?"}
    B -->|"no"| C{"🔀 Is any part<br/>of it known?"}
    B -->|"yes"| D{"🔀 Does it need resume<br/>or human approval?"}
    C -->|"no"| E(["🔁 Free loop + step cap"])
    C -->|"yes"| F(["🕸️ Graph, with a loop in the uncertain node"])
    D -->|"yes"| G(["🕸️ Explicit graph — checkpoint per node"])
    D -->|"no"| H{"🔀 More than a handful<br/>of edge cases?"}
    H -->|"yes"| F
    H -->|"no"| G

The branch that matters is "is any part of it known". Almost always some of it is — retrieval then analysis then formatting — and that partial structure is worth making explicit even when one stage inside it is a loop. All-or-nothing is a false choice and choosing it is how teams end up with a single unbounded loop.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Nobody wants to touch the graph. Every change breaks something unrelated."

Root cause. The team had started with an explicit graph, which was right. Then each production incident was fixed by adding a conditional edge to handle that specific case — a route for empty results, a route for a particular API's rate limit, a route for a malformed document type. Eighteen months in the graph had dozens of edges, most encoding a single historical failure, and no way to tell which were structural. Changes broke unrelated paths because the paths weren't independent, and nobody could safely delete an edge because nobody knew what it was for.

Fix. The incident-derived edges collapsed into two nodes, each containing a bounded loop with a clear success condition — "get usable results" and "parse this document" — so variation was handled by iteration rather than by structure. The graph went back to a readable shape. The lesson is that an edge should encode a decision, not an exception; exceptions belong inside a node.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

If you cap the loop anyway, what does the graph give you beyond that?

Named terminations. A step cap tells you the run stopped; it doesn't tell you whether it succeeded, failed, or ran out of budget mid-thought. A graph has terminal nodes with meanings — answered, escalated, abstained — so the outcome is a fact rather than an inference from the trace.

The second thing is the resume point. A cap has no notion of where you were; a graph checkpoints at node boundaries, so a crash or a human pause resumes from a known state rather than restarting. That's what makes long runs and approvals possible at all.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A graph can't take paths you didn't draw. Isn't that a serious capability ceiling?

It is, and it's the reason I don't put the whole system in one. But the ceiling applies to structure, not to behaviour — a node containing a bounded loop can do anything the model can think of, within that stage. What the graph fixes is the sequence of stages, which is usually the part that genuinely shouldn't vary.

The case where the ceiling really bites is genuine open-ended exploration, where even the stages aren't knowable. There I'd use a free loop and accept that the step cap is the only bound, while being explicit that I've traded testability for reach.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The graph now has forty nodes across three teams. What breaks?

Comprehension first, then testing. Nobody holds forty nodes in their head, so changes are made locally with no view of the whole, and the transition tests that made the graph trustworthy become the thing slowing every change down.

At that size I'd stop treating it as one graph. Sub-graphs with their own entry and exit contracts let a team own a region and test it in isolation, and the top-level graph becomes a small readable thing composing them. That mirrors what you'd do with any forty-function module, and the reason it's worth saying explicitly is that graph frameworks make it easy to keep adding nodes to one flat structure until it's unreadable.

The other thing that breaks is the checkpoint schema, because a node's state shape is now a cross-team contract. Versioning that deliberately — rather than discovering it during a deploy — is the boring work that keeps resume working.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design control flow for a system where product teams add capabilities weekly.

I'd fix the top-level graph as a platform concern and make capabilities pluggable nodes behind a contract: typed input, typed output, a declared max duration and a declared failure behaviour. Teams ship nodes, not edges — because edges are where coupling lives, and letting teams add edges is how the forty-node problem happens.

Routing between capabilities would be a decision node with a declarative policy rather than hand-drawn edges, so adding a capability means registering it with the conditions under which it applies. That keeps the structural change to a registry entry and keeps the graph's shape stable as the catalogue grows.

What I'd measure is path distribution over time. If nearly all traffic takes two paths out of twenty, the graph is carrying structure it doesn't need and should be pruned; if traffic is spread evenly across many, the routing policy is probably guessing and deserves a look before the graph grows further.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "A step cap makes a free loop safe enough — the graph is ceremony."

✅ Reality: A cap bounds cost, not correctness. It can't distinguish success from exhaustion, gives you no resume point, and leaves every transition untestable. Those are three different properties and the cap provides none of them.

❌ Trap: "Explicit graphs mean you've given up on agency."

✅ Reality: The graph fixes the stages; a node can contain a loop with full adaptivity inside it. The common production shape is explicit at the top and agentic inside one or two nodes, which keeps reliability where it's cheap and flexibility where it's needed.

❌ Trap: "Every new failure mode gets a new edge — that's the graph doing its job."

✅ Reality: An edge should encode a decision, not an exception. Exceptions encoded as structure produce a graph nobody can maintain or safely prune. Handle variation inside a node with a bounded loop and keep edges for choices that genuinely branch the flow.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • State Machines & Explicit Control Flow for Reliability — the reliability case for explicitness.

  • Durable Execution — Checkpointing, HITL Interrupts, Time Travel — what node boundaries enable.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Checkpoint every step — the node boundary is the checkpoint boundary.

  • §7 HITL as a durable pause — an interrupt needs an edge to pause at.

  • §8 Hard budgets — a graph bounds itself structurally; a free loop needs the cap.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — approval gates need explicit edges to pause on.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — the graph is the deliverable there.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Reflexion — verbal self-feedback, and the evaluator it depends on — Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning (arXiv 2303.11366)

  • Self-refine, and the limits of a model critiquing its own output — Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback (arXiv 2303.17651)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Reflexion & Self-Critique — the actor/evaluator/reflection mechanism.

  • Self-Refine-Iterative Improvement Loops — iterative refinement and where it plateaus.

What this note adds: the gating condition and the stopping rule. Reflexion's own design has an evaluator with a real signal; the decision is whether yours does, and if not, what the loop is actually buying.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The gate? Is the critique grounded in something checkable outside the model?
Ungrounded critic buys? A correlated second opinion, at double the cost per iteration.
The stopping rule? A fixed iteration cap plus a no-improvement exit. Never "until good".

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

A reflection loop is worth it when the critique is grounded — tests that run, a schema that validates, a query that returns rows. Then each iteration carries real information and the loop converges. When the critic is just another model call with no external signal, it shares the generator's blind spots, so I'm paying double per iteration for a correlated opinion and the loop tends to plateau after one pass. My rule is: ground the critique or skip the loop, and either way cap the iterations and exit on no-improvement rather than on the critic declaring satisfaction.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Grounded loop — tests, schema, execution A deterministic check exists and is cheap to run. Verification time per iteration; a sandbox to run it in. Code, SQL, structured output, anything executable.
Rubric critic with retrieval No execution, but claims can be checked against sources. Retrieval per iteration; partial grounding only. Research, summarisation with citations.
Self-critique, ungrounded Nothing external exists and you want one cleanup pass. ~2× per iteration for a correlated opinion; plateaus fast. Free-text where "better" is a matter of judgement.
No loop — single pass + escalate The output is judgement and being wrong is consequential. Human minutes; a review queue with an SLA. Support, advice, anything a human must sign off.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Grounded A cycle between generator and checker, plus an iteration cap. Each iteration is productive — cost buys measured progress. Iterations-to-pass is the health metric; a rise means quality drift.
Rubric + retrieval A critic node with its own retrieval path. Model call plus retrieval per iteration. Rubric drift needs its own eval; the critic is now a thing to version.
Ungrounded A second model call in a cycle. Doubles per iteration for an unverifiable gain. Hard to tell whether it's helping without a separate eval.
No loop Confidence scoring and an escalation path instead of a cycle. Cost moves from tokens to human minutes. The queue is the bottleneck, not the model.

The redraw test: a grounded loop puts a checker box in the cycle — a test runner, a validator, a query. If the cycle is two model boxes pointing at each other, that's the ungrounded case and the cost is real while the benefit isn't.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Adding a reviewer step doubled our cost and the eval scores didn't move."

Root cause. The team added a critic that read the generated answer and suggested improvements, with up to three refinement rounds. The critic was the same model with a reviewer prompt, reading the same context, so it agreed with the generator on everything they were both wrong about — which is precisely the set of cases the loop was supposed to catch. It did rewrite wording each round, so outputs changed and the loop looked like it was working, but the changes were stylistic. Eval scores were flat because nothing factual was being corrected.

Fix. The critic was replaced by citation resolution — every factual claim had to map to a retrieved span, which is deterministic — and unresolvable claims were stripped and the run escalated. One grounded check outperformed three ungrounded rounds at a third of the cost. The diagnostic that would have caught it earlier is simply measuring the loop's marginal value: score at iteration 1 versus iteration 3.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Reflexion & Self-Critique — the mechanism, including its evaluator.

  • llm-as-judge for trajectories — why a model judge correlates with the generator.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Is there a verifier — that answer is this note's gate.

  • §3 Which workflow shape — evaluator-optimizer is this decision as a shape.

  • §8 Verification gates — deterministic checks first, critic model last.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Coding agent — tests make this the easy, obviously-worth-it case.

  • §14 Deep research agent — citation resolution is the grounding that makes a critic useful.

notes.title: Adopt an orchestration framework or stay on the plain SDK
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§3 Control Flow & Orchestration)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • What a graph framework provides beyond the model SDK — state, checkpointing, interrupts — LangGraph: persistence

  • A code-first orchestration model, for contrast with graph-first — OpenAI Agents SDK: handoffs

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Framework vs No-Framework — the adoption trade-off in full.

  • Graph-based vs Role-based vs Code-first Orchestration — the three framework styles.

What this note adds: what you're actually buying, which is durability rather than orchestration. A loop is twenty lines; a correct checkpointer is not — so the adoption decision is really about whether you need resume, and the style choice follows from how your control flow is shaped.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What you're really buying? Durability — checkpointing, resume, interrupts. Not the loop.
When plain SDK is right? Short runs, no resume, no human pause. The loop is trivial to write.
What picks the style? Graph if flow is a state machine; code-first if it's ordinary control flow.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The orchestration loop is the cheap part — a while loop with a step cap is twenty lines and I'd rather own it. What a framework actually sells is durability: checkpoint per step, resume after a crash, interrupt for a human and come back days later. So the question isn't "framework or not", it's whether runs need to survive interruption. If they're short and synchronous, plain SDK and keep the dependency surface small. If they pause or crash-and-resume, adopt one, because a correct checkpointer is genuinely hard and nobody's first attempt handles concurrent branch writes.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Plain SDK + your own loop Short synchronous runs, no resume, no HITL. You own durability if you ever need it — and retrofitting is a rewrite. Runs in seconds; a single request/response.
Graph framework Flow is a state machine; you need checkpointing and interrupts. Their state model and their abstractions in your call stack. Named stages, approval pauses, long runs.
Code-first framework You want handoffs and tracing without modelling flow as a graph. Less structural guarantee — control flow is ordinary code again. Flow is naturally procedural; a graph feels like ceremony.
Role-based framework Prototyping a multi-agent idea quickly. Roles as a metaphor rather than a structure; hard to reason about at scale. You're exploring whether multi-agent helps at all.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Plain SDK Nothing beyond your own code. No state store implied. Zero framework overhead; you pay in engineering if requirements grow. You own everything, including the bugs — which are yours to fix immediately.
Graph framework A checkpoint store, a state schema, and node boundaries as structure. One state write per super-step. Framework upgrades become a risk; state schema needs migrations.
Code-first Tracing and handoff plumbing provided; flow stays in your code. Light. Less to migrate, less provided — durability may still be yours.
Role-based Agents as roles with a coordination layer between them. Multiplies calls as roles converse. Hard to debug: behaviour emerges from prompts rather than structure.

The redraw test: adopting a graph framework puts a checkpoint store in the diagram. If your picture doesn't gain one, you adopted a dependency for the loop — which you could have written.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We're spending more time working around the framework than the loop would have taken to write."

Root cause. A team adopted a graph framework for an agent with runs of a few seconds, no human approval, and no resume requirement. They needed none of the durability machinery, but they inherited the state model — every piece of data had to be expressed as graph state with reducers, including things that were plainly local variables. Their actual control flow was three sequential steps, which the graph expressed more verbosely than a function would have, and framework upgrades broke their state schema twice.

Fix. They moved to the plain SDK with a small loop and kept one dependency for tracing. The lesson isn't that frameworks are bad — it's that the thing they sell is durability, and a team that doesn't need durability is paying the abstraction cost for none of the benefit.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Framework vs No-Framework — the adoption trade-off.

  • Durable Execution — Checkpointing, HITL Interrupts, Time Travel — the thing you're buying.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §3 Graph or free loop — the style choice follows the shape of your control flow.

  • §7 Durable execution — this decision is largely that requirement, arriving early.

  • §13 Build vs buy — the same question at platform scale.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — long pauses make durability non-negotiable.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — the framework choice becomes a platform-wide commitment.

notes.title: A reasoning model for the planning step
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§3 Control Flow & Orchestration)
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Reasoning models and where their extra inference time pays off — OpenAI: reasoning models guide

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Reasoning models as agents — what reasoning models do differently and where they help.

  • TOT — tree search as an explicit alternative to a stronger single call.

What this note adds: the placement — reasoning models buy fewer, better steps at the cost of slower ones, which is a good trade at exactly one point in the loop.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Where does it pay? The planning step. One slow call that removes several fast wrong ones.
Where does it not? Per-step execution — you pay latency on every step for little gain.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I'd use a reasoning model for the one call where the decomposition happens, and a fast model everywhere else. The trade is fewer steps for slower steps, and that only nets out where a better decision removes downstream work — which is planning. Using one for every step in the loop pays the latency tax repeatedly for decisions that don't need it. Tree-of-Thoughts style search is the same idea made explicit: spend more compute to pick a better path, worth it when a wrong path is expensive and the budget allows.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Reasoning model at the planner only Decomposition quality drives the whole run. One slow, expensive call per run. Plans are the thing that goes wrong.
Reasoning model throughout Every step involves hard judgement — rare. Latency on every step; usually a poor trade. You genuinely can't identify a cheap step.
Fast model + explicit search (ToT) A wrong path is costly and you can evaluate partial paths. N× the calls for the search breadth. You have a scoring function for partial solutions.
Fast model everywhere Steps are simple and the plan is short. Weaker plans, recovered by a repair loop. The default until a plan-quality problem shows up.
